ACTS: Stocks from the US and abroad, including emerging markets, with technology and industrials the biggest slices at about half combined. The managers shift the mix tactically as conditions change, making it an actively steered global stock holding rather than a set-and-forget index fund.
AINT: US large-company stocks held long and short in roughly equal dollar amounts, with positions chosen by an AI-driven process. Because the longs and shorts offset, it aims to profit from picking winners over losers regardless of the market's direction, a hedge-style holding rather than a growth engine.
BAGY: Bitcoin exposure paired with an aggressive call-selling program designed to squeeze out as much income as possible. The sold calls can hand much of bitcoin's upside to the option buyers, so it suits income seekers while still falling hard when bitcoin drops.
BGEG: Actively managed growth companies across emerging markets, with technology near half, run by a firm known for backing future winners early. It is a high-conviction growth bet on developing economies, so it can pull well ahead of or behind the broad emerging-market pack.
BRAZ: Brazilian companies picked actively, led by banks at over a third, with energy, industry and miners behind. It is a single-country bet on Latin America's largest economy, where commodity prices, politics and the currency can all swing the fund hard.
CBIL: US Treasury bills that come due in three to twelve months, the shortest and safest corner of the bond market. It is a cash-like parking spot that pays a bit more than a savings account, with essentially no credit risk and very little price movement.
CCML: Makers of multilayer ceramic capacitors and other electronic components, the tiny parts that sit inside nearly every phone, car and computer. It is a narrow bet on one corner of the chip supply chain most investors never see, so it rides electronics demand and factory cycles in Asia especially.
CPII: A toolkit for fighting inflation: inflation-protected Treasury bonds plus inflation swaps and interest-rate options, actively arranged by the managers. It is built to gain when inflation heats up or investors start expecting more of it, so it works as a hedge rather than a steady income holding.
DGIN: Indian companies building the country's digital economy: telecom networks, online shopping, payments and software services. It is a focused growth bet on hundreds of millions of Indians coming online, in a single-country fund that will swing with India's market and currency.
DIPS: Options that bet against chipmaker Nvidia while selling other options to pay out income, backed by Treasury bills. It is designed to profit, in part, when Nvidia falls and to keep paying distributions either way, an unusual bearish income play on a single very popular stock.
DIVG: Companies from the S&P 500 picked for the fastest expected growth in their dividends, led by banks at nearly a third, with utilities and food and household staples next. It blends income with dividend growth, aiming for payouts that rise over time rather than the biggest yields today.
EBIT: Small US companies that actually make money, screened for profits rather than promises, with banks the biggest group at over a quarter. It skips the many small stocks that have never earned a profit, aiming for a steadier version of small-company growth.
EFZ: A trading tool that bets against large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, aiming to move opposite to them each day. The daily reset makes longer results drift from a simple mirror image, so it is built for short-term hedges and trades, not holding.
ENHU: Large US companies picked by computer models that forecast returns, staying close to the Russell 1000 so results rarely stray far from the broad market. It is an enhanced core holding: mostly index-like, with small active tilts meant to add a little extra over time.
FDTS: Small companies in developed markets outside the US, in Europe, Japan and elsewhere, screened by a scoring system for price and growth traits, with industrials the biggest group. It hunts for overlooked foreign small caps, adding currency swings and thinner trading to the usual small-stock risks.
FMKT: US companies the managers expect to benefit when regulation loosens, spread across banking, industry, technology and health care. It is a policy bet as much as a stock bet: it should do best when Washington is cutting rules for heavily regulated industries.
GCPU: Data-center and computing companies that grew out of bitcoin mining: AI cloud operators, hosting firms and miners that rent out heavy computing power. The same server farms increasingly serve artificial intelligence workloads, so the fund sits where crypto mining meets the AI buildout, with swings to match.
GDT: Two inflation defenses stacked together: inflation-protected Treasury bonds and gold futures, layered so each dollar does double duty. It is built for savers worried about rising prices eroding their cash, pairing the government's inflation adjustment with gold's long record as a crisis asset.
HLTH: Companies applying artificial intelligence to health care: drug discovery platforms, medical imaging, diagnostics and hospital software, from the US and abroad. It is a theme bet where two fast-moving fields meet, so it carries both biotech-style swings and tech-style enthusiasm.
IBMX: Municipal bonds that mature around 2035, paying interest free of federal income tax and the alternative minimum tax. The fund is designed to wind up near the end of 2035 and hand the money back, making it a date-certain holding for a goal in that year.
ION: Companies around the world that mine the metals batteries are made from: lithium, cobalt and nickel. It is a focused bet on battery demand from electric vehicles and energy storage, sitting further up the supply chain than the carmakers, so metal prices drive it.
IPOS: Newly public companies from outside the US, bought soon after their stock market debuts and held for their first years of trading. It is a growth bet on fresh listings, which can soar early and fade fast, so it is far jumpier than a seasoned foreign stock fund.
JHDV: US large and mid-sized companies that pay dividends, though technology is the biggest slice at nearly half thanks to the cash-rich tech giants. It aims for income from household-name stocks, so it behaves more like a core stock holding than a traditional yield fund heavy in utilities.
JHID: Dividend-paying companies from developed markets outside the US, led by banks at about a third, in Europe, Japan and other rich economies. It is an income-focused foreign stock holding, pairing payouts with diversification away from the US market and its currency swings.
JLCO: Large US companies picked actively across technology, consumer brands, health care and banking, hunting for underpriced opportunities among household names. It is a stock-picker's core holding, aiming to beat the broad large-company market rather than match it, so results depend on the manager's calls.
KPHO: Stocks listed in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, dominated by banks at about three-quarters of the fund. It is a single-country frontier-market bet on a fast-growing manufacturing economy, with the extra risks of a small market, currency moves and limits on foreign ownership.
LAPR: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay an income stream while absorbing the first slice of market losses named in the fund's title. It is built for investors who want stock-market-linked income with a cushion, trading away most upside and renewing its terms each period, with this series starting in April.
LOCT: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay an income stream while absorbing the first slice of market losses named in the fund's title. It is built for investors who want stock-market-linked income with a cushion, trading away most upside and renewing its terms each period, with this series starting in October.
MATR: A mix of stock, bond and other funds, mostly US equities at about seven-tenths, rebalanced as the managers read global conditions. It is a one-fund portfolio for hands-off investors, trading the precision of building your own mix for professional allocation decisions.
MPDB: Large US stock exposure through swaps on a special buffer index that adjusts its protection level as market conditions change. It aims to soften the first slice of losses while keeping some upside, a cushion-style equity holding whose protection is recalculated rather than fixed.
MYMK: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that mostly come due in 2031, paying interest that is exempt from regular federal income tax. It suits savers aiming at a goal around 2031, with tax-free income along the way and risk that eases as the bonds near their due dates.
PEX: Publicly traded private equity firms from around the world: the big buyout shops whose shares anyone can buy. It offers stock-market access to the buyout business without the long lockups of private funds, though these shares swing like the financial stocks they are.
PQNT: Stocks from developed markets outside the US, led by banks at about a third and industrial companies next, picked with help from artificial intelligence models. It is a core-style foreign stock holding with a machine-guided twist, aiming to beat plain international indexes rather than simply match them.
QBQF: Growth-company exposure in the style of the Nasdaq-100, mostly technology at about three-fifths, built with options that absorb the first 15% of losses over each outcome period, the level in its name. Gains are capped in exchange, so it is a cushioned way to hold fast-growing stocks.
QTR: The companies of the Nasdaq-100 plus protective put options bought to blunt a sharp market crash. The insurance costs a steady drag in calm markets, so it is a growth holding with a built-in airbag for investors who fear a sudden tech-led sell-off.
RDOG: The highest-dividend-paying real estate investment trusts in the US, picked segment by segment from property types like apartments, malls, warehouses and cell towers. High payouts are the whole point, but chasing the biggest yields can mean owning the landlords whose prices fell hardest.
RIZE: Short-term inflation-protected bonds, mostly US Treasury TIPS whose principal rises with consumer prices. It is a defensive parking spot meant to keep pace with inflation over short stretches, giving up the higher yields of longer or riskier bonds for stability.
RSMR: Options on an equal-weighted version of the S&P 500, where the smallest company counts as much as the largest, wrapped in a buffer over a period ending in March. The equal weighting tilts away from mega-cap tech, and the buffer absorbs the first slice of losses while gains are capped.
STAX: Short-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, chosen so the interest stays free of federal income tax, including the alternative minimum tax. Short maturities keep price swings small, making it a tax-smart parking spot for cash that will be needed soon.
TAPR: S&P 500 exposure wrapped in options designed to protect against losses over the two-year period ending in April 2027, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is built for cautious investors who want stock-market participation with a defined safety net, provided they hold for the full period.
TJUN: Options on a broad emerging-markets fund that give a buffered ride on stocks in China, Taiwan, India and other developing economies over a period ending in June. The buffer absorbs the first slice of losses while gains are capped, softening a famously bouncy corner of the market.
TMID: Mid-sized US companies across technology, industry, health care and banking, chosen using the firm's own analyst research. It plays the middle of the market, between big blue chips and small caps, as an actively managed core-style holding built from the firm's stock-by-stock views.
TOT: Broad US stock exposure built from other index funds, arranged to keep taxable distributions to a minimum. It aims to deliver the market's total return in a more tax-efficient wrapper, which matters most in taxable accounts where yearly payouts create a tax bill.
UTRE: A single holding: the most recently issued three-year US Treasury note, replaced as new notes are auctioned. It is a precise building block for investors managing interest-rate exposure year by year, paying government-backed income with modest sensitivity to rate moves.
UXJA: Options on the S&P 500 that multiply the market's gains over a year-long period ending in January, with a built-in buffer against the first slice of losses. The trade-off is weaker results in flat markets and losses beyond the buffer, so it is an amplified, time-boxed way to bet on rising stocks.
VBCH: Corporate bonds from US companies chosen to mature around 2034, when the fund is designed to wrap up and return its cash. It is a date-targeted income holding for a goal in that year, carrying company credit risk and interest-rate risk that shrinks as 2034 approaches.
WDAF: Defense companies across Asia: shipbuilders, aerospace firms and military suppliers in countries like Japan, South Korea and India. It is a focused bet on Asian governments raising military budgets, with the political and currency risks of a single-theme regional fund.
WRND: Companies from around the world chosen for how heavily they invest in research and development, led by technology at about three-fifths. The idea is that today's research spending becomes tomorrow's products and profits, making this a growth holding built on innovation budgets.
WSMD: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by Wasatch's research team, hunting for quality growers before they become household names. It is an active growth holding in the market's middleweight division, where stock picking matters more and swings run bigger than in large caps.
YSAU: Physical gold bars held in vaults, so the fund's price follows the metal itself rather than mining companies or futures. It is the classic crisis and inflation hedge in fund form, paying no income and moving with whatever investors will pay for gold.
